title: The two-list experiment
task: Study list A by rereading it three times. Study list B by reading it once, covering it, writing the words you recall, then checking - and repeating that loop twice. Tomorrow, recall both lists from memory and compare the counts.

checks.prompt: For list B, did you read once, cover it, write your recall, then check - and repeat that loop twice?
The next day, did you write down what you recalled from each list before looking at either file?
Did you record how many words survived from list A and from list B?

hints.text: The comparison only means something if each list gets a different method and roughly equal attention.
Recall attempts during study are the entire difference between the two lists.

solution: Read list A three times. For list B: read once, cover, recall, check - twice. Tomorrow: recall both cold, count the survivors, compare.

title: Audit your highlights
task: Pick a chapter you highlighted at least a week ago. With the book closed, write everything you remember in cairn-recall-notes.txt. Then reopen the chapter and check your highlights against what you wrote.

checks.prompt: Did you write your recall before reopening the chapter?
Did you mark which highlights match things you produced from memory, and which do not?
Did you write one line estimating what share of the highlighted material actually survived?

hints.text: The audit measures the highlights, not you. Whatever number you get is the finding.
If most highlights mark things you did not recall, the highlighting trained recognition, not recall.

solution: Recall first with notes closed, then check against the highlights, then write your survival estimate.

title: Spacing audit
task: For one week, log every contact you have with the material you are learning in cairn-spacing-log.txt: the date, and whether the contact was new learning, rereading, or recall from memory. At the end of the week, audit the pattern.

checks.prompt: Were there gaps of at least one day between some contacts, or did everything happen in the same evening?
Did you count how many contacts were recall from memory rather than rereading?
Did you write the next two review dates, at expanding intervals?

hints.text: Same-day sessions cluster. The spacing effect lives in the gaps between days.
A log entry is one line: date, material, and whether you recalled or re-exposed.

solution: Log date, material, and contact type for a week, then audit the gaps and the share of recall contacts, then set two expanding review dates.

title: Teach one thing back
task: Pick one thing you learned this week. With notes closed, explain it aloud for two minutes as if teaching it, then draw a quick sketch of it. After both, open your notes and write the gaps you found in cairn-teach-notes.txt.

checks.prompt: Did you explain aloud for two minutes with notes fully closed?
Did you draw the sketch yourself rather than copying one?
Did you write down where you got stuck, then check the notes for exactly those points?

hints.text: The pauses and stumbles are the data. They mark exactly where encoding was thin.
If the explanation went smoothly, pick a harder topic and repeat.

solution: Explain cold for two minutes, sketch from memory, then hunt the notes only for the points where you stumbled.
